interface_note: Only parameter values vary; all mathematical conditions and requested quantity remain those stated by the supplied source questions. Names describe source data, not a target algorithm. Implement solve(parameters), no natural-language applicability detection. max_length must not exceed the number of distinct supplied digits.

observations: All source tasks share one structure: given a set of distinct digits and a maximum length L (here 4), count distinct primes formable by choosing k digits (1<=k<=L), permuting without repetition, with no leading zero.

The failures are arithmetic/enumeration errors: truncated manual primality checks, guessed 4-digit counts, and inconsistent per-length subtotals. The mathematical procedure is deterministic and fully checkable.

Key correctness constraints: deduplicate results (different digit selections cannot yield the same integer because digit multisets differ, but dedupe defensively), enforce no leading zero, and test primality exactly by trial division up to floor(sqrt(n)).

Pruning is safe and exact: for k>=2 the last digit must be in {1,3,7,9}; reject candidates whose digit sum is divisible by 3 (for n>3); single-digit primes are exactly {2,3,5,7} intersected with the digit set.
max_length must be clamped to at most the number of distinct supplied digits; k ranges over 1..min(max_length, len(digits)).
analysis.procedure_plan: solve(parameters): read digits (dedupe, keep as ints) and max_length; set L=min(max_length, len(digits)). Initialize a set S of primes. For k=1..L: enumerate all ordered k-tuples of distinct digits (permutations of size k from the digit set). For each tuple: if k>1 and first digit is 0, skip; build integer n; if k==1, include n iff n in {2,3,5,7}; else skip if last digit not in {1,3,7,9}; skip if digit sum % 3 == 0; otherwise test primality by trial division d=2,3,5,... while d*d<=n (increment by 1 or use 6k±1), and add n to S if prime. Return len(S). Use exact integer arithmetic; no floating point. Optionally memoize primality tests.
analysis.uncertainty: Low mathematical uncertainty: the procedure is a direct exhaustive enumeration with exact primality testing, so it is correct for any digit set and max_length within the schema. The only practical concern is runtime for large digit sets, but with at most 10 digits and max_length 4 the search space is at most sum_{k=1..4} P(10,k) ~ 5860 candidates, trivially fast. No reliance on the failed trajectories' guessed counts.
